title: Combined work rates
transcript: A work rate tells you how much of one complete job is done per unit of time. If one worker takes six minutes, the rate is one sixth of the job each minute. Workers on the same job contribute their rates. An activity that undoes progress subtracts from that total rate.

In AMC practice, filling tanks, packing boxes or shared work can be described by the time for a whole task. Rewrite that time as progress per minute. A Rossmoyne style problem might change workers part of the way through. Split the timeline and keep the remaining work.
A machine labels a whole batch of boxes in ten minutes at a steady rate. What fraction of the batch does it label in one minute? Use equal parts of the job.
Divide the batch into ten equal portions. One minute is one of those portions. The rate is one over ten of a batch per minute. Multiply this fraction by ten minutes to check it gives one batch.
Machine A can finish one batch in ten minutes. Machine B takes fifteen minutes to finish a batch of the same size. How long does one batch take if they work together at their full rates?

Represent one batch by thirty units. A completes three units per minute, and B completes two. The combined rate is five units per minute. Both machines contribute during the same minute. The time is thirty divided by five. That is six minutes.

Two pumps together fill a tank. Alone, one would take ten minutes and the other fifteen minutes. After four minutes a leak opens which would empty a full tank in thirty minutes by itself. How long from the start until the tank is full?

Use thirty units for a full tank. The pumps initially fill five units per minute, so they add twenty before the leak. That leaves ten units. The leak removes one unit each minute, so the new net rate is four units per minute. Divide the remaining work by four, then add the initial four minutes. The answer is thirteen over two minutes.

The first period contributes twenty units. During the second period, the net addition is ten units. The two contributions fill exactly one tank. The two different rates apply to two different time intervals.

Times for a whole job do not add when two workers are working at once. Convert both times to rates before adding. A leak running during the second period has no effect on the first period's work. Keep the rate with its own interval.

Choose a convenient number of units for the job. A common multiple of the given times often gives whole-number rates. After every change, subtract completed work from the whole. Use the new net rate only for the remaining work.
